The drug profile is updated per the hospice policy and procedure, but, at minimum, at the time of each comprehensive assessment and/or when new medication is added, or changes are made to existing medication.
 
This standard was not met as evidenced by clinical record review, document review, and interview. In 1 of 14 (7%) records reviewed. the agency did not ensure the drug profile was updated per hospice policy and procedure. 

Agency policy PC.M60, Medication - Profile, stated in part, "When a patient is admitted to hospice, a medication profile is initiated to document all of the patient's prescription and over the counter drugs, herbal remedies and alternative supplements tat could affect drug therapy. The patient's medication profile is reviewed by the IDG whenever there is a significant change and, at a minimum every 15 days.  The patient medication profile review includes but is not limited to: determining accuracy and completeness of the profile."

Clinical Record 1: The updated hospice plan of care dated 6/28/23 read in part, "O2 @ 2-4L via NC." The licensed practical nurse visit note dated 7/5/23, and the registered nurse visit note dated 6/27/23, stated oxygen use at "4L via NC."  However, oxygen was not included on the medication profile, with documented review dates by the registered nurse on 6/28/23 and 7/1/23.

During an interview on 7/13/23, the QA Nurse confirmed the finding.

Additionally verbalized process for employee screening for COVID failed to be documented after 11/30/2021.  The lack of the COVID documentation has potential risk of communicable disease spreading (L581).

The cumulative effect of these systemic problems resulted in the hospice agency's inability to ensure the provision of quality health care in a safe environment.

It is required that if a patient revokes the election of hospice care or is discharged from hospice per hospice regulation §418.26 (i.e., no longer terminally ill), the hospice forwards to the patient’s attending physician a copy of the hospice discharge summary.

This standard was not met as evidenced by clinical record review and interview. In 1 of 1 (100%) discharged clinical records reviewed in which the patient revoked services, the organization did not ensure that a discharge summary was forwarded to the patient's attending physician. 

CLINICAL RECORD 15: The patient elected the hospice benefit on 02/16/2026 with a primary terminal diagnosis of diastolic (congestive) heart failure and revoked services to seek aggressive treatment on 03/02/2026. During a joint clinical record review and interview on 09/11/2026, the Administrator and Directors of Patient Services confirmed that they never sent a discharge summary to the patient's primary practitioner. The Administrator stated that the organization discovered in July (2026) that discharge summaries were not being automatically faxed to the primary practitioners of patients discharged alive from hospice services as required by regulations. The Administrator stated, "After our acquisition, we were told that our live discharge summaries would be faxed to primary practitioners. We learned recently that our Team Coordinators were responsible for this process. They have been taught to send all Discharge/Transfer Summary Reports to Primary Care physicians and skilled nursing facilities as of July of this year. That's why this patient's discharge was not sent to the patient's physician."

It is required that a patient clinical record containing past and current findings is maintained for each hospice patient.  The record contains correct clinical information that is available to the patient’s attending physician and hospice staff.  The record may be maintained electronically or on paper. Each patient’s record includes, at a minimum:  Physician orders.

Agency Policy TX.16 Medication Administration and Management (Revised 082115) stated in part, "Agency nurse will obtain physician orders...A written physician order is obtained for medication...." 1 of 12 (16%) records in which additional physician orders were required failed to document a physician order for medications.

Record #27815:  Nursing visit note 11/20/2021 documented Doxycycline [medication to treat a bacterial infection] was discontinued and started Azithromycin [medication to treat a bacterial infection] 250mg orally two tablets then one tablet daily for four days, no physician order as of review 12/28/2021.  Nursing visit note 12/07/2021 documented Robitussin [medication to decrease cough] started for patient cough.  No physician order was documented as of review 12/28/2021.

Interview with the Area Vice President of Operations and Patient Care Manager stated that they agreed, physician orders were not documented correctly for a patient in a skilled facility.

It is required that a patient clinical record containing past and current findings is maintained for each hospice patient. The record contains correct clinical information that is available to the patient’s attending physician and hospice staff.  The record may be maintained electronically or on paper. Each patient’s record includes, at a minimum:  The initial plan of care, updated plans of care, initial assessment, comprehensive assessment, updated comprehensive assessments, and clinical notes, including the care and services provided. 

This standard was not met as evidenced by a review of clinical records, document review, and interview.  Agency Policy IM.7 (revised 1.1.2020) Medical Record Format stated in part, "Active Medical Record:  Nursing, communication notes." 1 of 14 (07%) records failed to include all communication notes for the care provided to the patient.

Record #66344:  Nursing communication note on 04/27/2021 documented that orders were obtained from a physician for a potassium lab draw.  Nursing visit note 05/03/2021 documented attempted lab draw with three unsuccessful attempts.  Documentation on nursing visit note stated that caregiver stated that the patient is a very difficult draw and requires vascular to draw blood.  The record failed to document a communication note of how the lab was drawn and follow up for the lab draw prior to the revocation on 05/16/2021.

Interview with the Area Vice President of Operations and the Patient Care Manager stated that the communication note should have documented the access to vascular for the lab draw and follow-through for the lab draw.

text_segments.text: Based on the review of medical records (MR), policy and procedure, observations, and interviews, it was determined the agency failed to ensure a current, accurate medication profile was available in the MR. This affected one of three home visits (HV), including HV # 2, and had the potential to negatively affect all patients served by the agency. Findings include: Policy: Medication ProfilePolicy Number: 2-004Purpose: To define the use of the medication profile in evaluating a patient's medication regimen.Policy: Patients receiving medications... will have a current, accurate medication profile in the medical record. The medication profiles will be updated for each change to reflect current medications, and new and/or discontinued medications.Procedure:  1. Upon admission to hospice, the admitting nurse will initiate a medication profile to document the current medication regimen... 2. A drug regimen review will be performed at the time of initial and comprehensive assessment, when updates to the comprehensive assessment are performed, when care is resumed after a patient has been placed on hold, and with the addition of a new medication... 3. During subsequent HVs, the medication profile will be used as a care planning and teaching guide to ensure the patient and family/caregiver, as well as other clinicians, understand the medication regimen...      5. Based on review of the medication profile... changes in the plan of care may be required... 7. Deviations from taking medications as ordered will be documented in the MR, and the physician... will be notified.

HV # 2 was admitted to the agency on 5/28/25 with the primary diagnosis of Hypertensive Heart Disease with Heart Failure. A HV was conducted on 7/23/25 at 9:20 AM with Employee Identifier (EI) # 3, Hospice Aide, to observe care provided in the home. During the HV, the surveyor and the caregiver (CG), reviewed the Client Medication Report (CMR). The following discrepancies were observed:Allopurinol 300 milligram (mg) tablet, take 1 tablet by mouth (PO) daily, was available in the home and was listed as current on the CMR. The CG stated that HV # 2 has not taken the medication for "a couple of months."Atorvastatin 80 mg tablet, take 1 tablet PO daily, was available in the home. The medication was listed as discontinued on the CMR but the CG stated HV # 2 still takes it daily. An interview was conducted on 7/24/25 at 12:11 PM with EI # 1, Manager of Regulatory Compliance and Accreditation, who confirmed the CMR was not current or accurate.

text_segments.text: Based on review of policy titled “Physicians Orders – Verbal Orders,” review of records, and staff interviews, it was determined the agency failed to obtain physicians orders for treatment provided to two patients (P) (P#1 and P#3) of three sampled patients.

Findings include: Review of policy titled " Physicians Orders – Verbal Orders," revised March 2013 revealed the following:POLICY:  Drugs and treatments are administered by Hospice staff only as ordered by the physician. Only authorized staff receives and record verbal orders. Verbal orders are put in writing and signed and dated by the RN (or qualified therapists) responsible for furnishing or supervising the care.PURPOSE: To document verbal orders received from the patient's physician. 1. Review of the clinical records reveal P#1 was admitted to hospice on 1/20/26. The skilled nurse (SN) admitted the patient on 1/20/26 and provided wound care to sacral wound. The clinical record failed to include a physician's order for the wound care provided.During an interview on 2/11/26 at 2:00 p.m., the Administrator confirmed the SN failed to obtain a physician's order for the wound care provided. 2. Review of the clinical records reveal P#3 was admitted to hospice on 8/30/25 with a suprapubic catheter (flexible tube surgically inserted in the bladder to drain urine) and a colostomy system (a surgically created opening in the stomach so waste can exit the body and into a changeable pouch/bag).  The skilled nurse (SN) visit notes dated 1/13/26 and 2/3/26 indicate the suprapubic catheter was changed using a 24 French catheter. Documentation by the SN on 1/13/26 revealed that the suprapubic catheter has been leaking since admission and the SN packed area with gauze to prevent saturation.  Additionally, the SN documented on 1/13/26 that the colostomy bag is replaced 2 times a week. Review of the clinical record failed to include a physician's order for the catheter change or packing the catheter area and for the care and maintenance of the colostomy bag. During an interview with the Administrator on 2/11/26 at 11:30 a.m., it was confirmed the clinical record did not contain an order for catheter and colostomy care. The Administrator also stated the SN must obtain verbal or written orders from the physician prior to performing any care for the patient.

The following reflects the findings of the California Department of Public Health during an initial Certification Survey conducted on 9/1/22. 

The unduplicated admissions since the agency's inception was 8, the active census was 3. The team conducted 3 home visits with record review and 2 closed record reviews.

Representing the California Department of Public Health: 34383, Health Facilities Evaluator Supervisor; 38243, Health Facilities Evaluator Nurse; and 39238, Health Facilities Evaluator Nurse.

text_segments.text:
Based on observation, interview, and record review, the agency failed to ensure an individualized plan of care established by the hospice interdisciplinary group (IDG, the team responsible for the development and review of the hospice beneficiary's plan of care) for one of three sampled patient (Patient 2) when the physician order was not followed for oxygen (a chemical element found in the air as a colorless odorless tasteless gas that is necessary for life) at 2 liters continuously.

This failure had the potential to insufficient care provided to Patient 2.

Findings:

A review of Patient 2's IDG physician order with a start of care of 7/14/2022 indicated to give oxygen at 2 liters continuously for shortness of breath and comfort.

During a home visit observation for Patient 2 on 8/29/2022 at 2:30 p.m., it was observed the Director of Patient Care Services (DPCS) was providing care and Patient 2 do not have oxygen.

During an interview with the DPCS on 8/30/2022 at 10:40 a.m., she confirmed Patient 2 did not have an oxygen and physician order should have been followed.

Review of the agency's policy and procedure dated 10/2019, "Verification of Physician Orders", indicated orders will be obtained from a licensed physician (or other authorized independent practitioner) for care and services to be provided to hospice patients.

Based on interview and record review the agency failed to maintain a current medication profile for one (1) out of three (3) home visit patients (Patient 3). 

This failure puts Patient 3 at risk for adverse medication side effects. 

Findings: 

During a home visit on 8/30/22 at 2:00 p.m. with Patient 3 and Registered Nurse A (RN A), a medication review of Patient 3's current medications was conducted. The medication list printed on 8/29/22 was reviewed with the patient's care giver (CG 3), with RN A and with the medication list in the home.

The following medications and supplements had discrepancies: Concurrent interviews with both RN A and CG 3 confirmed these discrepancies. 
a. Ambien 5 milligrams (mg, a unit of measure) oral tablets started on 8/13/22 was not on the home medication list. This was confirmed by RN A.
b. Medihoney Wound/Burn Dressing External Gel started on 8/6/22. CG 3 stated medication was no longer used and they still have the medication at home. RN A stated this was for a wound on patient's back, but Patient 3 had no wound at the back.
c. Tramadol 50 mg oral tablets started on 4/21/2022. RN A stated he had it before, but he does not need it, Patient 3 gets Gabapentin now. CG 3 did not want to keep it.
d. Zinc Oxide External Ointment started on 3/13/2022. RN A stated this was for Patient 3's rash on the scrotum which resolved. Both RN A and CG 3 stated this was not used and it was only for 7 days. 
e. Ensure can and CG 3 stated she also gives Patient 3 Ensure 2 cans per day, but this was not on the list. 
f. Multivitamins (MVI) and CG 3 stated she also gives MVI to Patient 3 but it was not on the list. 

Concurrent interviews with both the CG 3 and RN A on 8/30/22 both confirmed the above observation and record review. 

Review of agency's Medication Profile Policy No. 2-004 dated October 2019, indicated the medication profiles will be updated for each change to reflect current medications, and new and/or discontinued medications.

A review of the clinical record of Patient #6 revealed a document titled, Aide Care Visit dated 08/08/23 from 8:05 AM to 9:30 AM, signed by HHA (Home Health Aide) 1, evidenced a complete bed bath was performed.  
During an observation on 08/08/23 at 8:30 AM, HHA 1 was to provide a bed bath for Patient #6.  Upon arrival, Patient #6 was observed in the patients bathroom, standing at the sink, next to their wheelchair, with their pants down to their knees, and a pair of adult diapers on.  Patient #6 asked HHA 1 for assistance.  HHA 1 assisted Patient #6 to their wheelchair, then onto the toilet, where a bath took place from 8:30 to 9:30 AM.
On 08/10/23 at 10:38 AM during a phone interview with HHA 1 indicated Patient #6 was terrified of showers, and since HHA 1 has been providing personal care, most days, a sponge bath was given instead of showers, and did not report to RN 2 changes to the care plan on 08/08/23.

When this writer told RN 2 of the observed home visit, they stated they would have to readdress the Aide Care Plan, and they had not spoken with HHA 1 since 08/03/23.

Based on review of agency policy, clinical records (CR), quality assessment and performance improvement (QAPI) data, and staff (EMP) interview, the agency failed to measure, analyze, and track quality indicators, including adverse patient events, and other aspects of performance that enable the hospice to assess processes of care, hospice services and operations for three (3) of four (4) active records who were prescribed antibiotics for infections (adverse patient event) (CR1, CR9, & CR10).

Findings included:

Review of agency policy on December 17, 2021, at 1 p.m. showed, "QUALITY ASSESSMENT AND PERFORMANCE IMPROVEMENT - Policy ... Data Sources to be used to monitor performance and to identify opportunities for improvement include, but are not limited to the following components of the organization and available data sources: ... Infection prevention surveillance and reporting."

Review of clinical records was conducted on December 14, 2021, and December 16, 2021 with EMP1 (administrator). 

Review of CR1 on December 14, 2021, at 12:30 p.m. showed patient was admitted on 11/5/2021 for an initial certification period ending 2/2/2022. On 12/5/2021, CR1 was prescribed Levaquin (antibiotic) for pneumonia (lung infection). Per 12/5/2021 nursing visit note, "ADDED THE LEVAQUIN ORDERED BY ER [emergency room] FOR ASPIRATION PNEUMONIA."

Review of CR9 on December 16, 2021, at 10:15 a.m. showed patient was admitted on 5/19/2021 with a recertification period of 11/15/2021 to 1/13/2022. On 8/31/2021, and again on 12/16/2021, the patient was prescribed azithromycin (antibiotic) for respiratory infections. Per the 8/31/2021 nursing visit note, "Lungs diminished with wheezes noted ... Patient reports dyspnea [shortness of breath] increasing secondary to congestion. Sputum thin to thick in nature and yellow tinged. Patient's wife asking for z-pack [azithromycin] as that is what they had to do in the past to clear it up secondary to his trach." 

Review of CR10 on December 16, 2021, at 10:45 a.m. showed patient was admitted on 2/1/2021 with a recertification period of 11/28/2021 to 1/26/2022. Per coordination note, "Rcvd [received] call from [SNF RN] supervisor late Friday 12/3/2021. Patient acting differently wondering if could be UTI, ... [physician] ordered UA [urinalysis] C & S [culture and sensitivity], discussed with [SNF RN] ... we can treat symptoms and cover ABX [antibiotic] if feel there is UTI." On 12/4/2021, the patient was prescribed Cipro (antibiotic) for a UTI (urinary tract infection). 

Review of QAPI and "Infection Prevention Audit List" with EMP1 on December 17, 2021, at 10:30 a.m. confirmed agency's QAPI was not aware of the above patient infections for the purpose of improving processes of patient care. The list included parameters for patient name, type of infection and if and antibiotic was ordered.

Interview with EMP1 on December 17, 2021, at 10:30 a.m. confirmed above findings and that infections are tracked and trended in QAPI per above audit list, but that CR1, CR9 and CR10's infections were not listed since agency staff had not reported them.

text_segments.text:
According to § 418.22 (b)(3), "Certification of terminal illness. ... (3) The physician must include a brief narrative explanation of the clinical findings that supports a life expectancy of 6 months or less as part of the certification and recertification forms, or as an addendum to the certification and recertification forms. (i) If the narrative is part of the certification or recertification form, then the narrative must be located immediately prior to the physician's signature. (ii) If the narrative exists as an addendum to the certification or recertification form, in addition to the physician's signature on the certification or recertification form, the physician must also sign immediately following the narrative in the addendum. (iii) The narrative shall include a statement directly above the physician signature attesting that by signing, the physician confirms that he/she composed the narrative based on his/her review [emphasis] of the patient's medical record or, if applicable, his/her examination of the patient."

Based on review of a clinical (CR), and interviews with nursing staff (EMP) and the medical director (MD), the agency failed to ensure the physician composed the narrative for initial certification of terminal illness based on his/her review (emphasis) of the clinical record or examination of the patient in accordance with § 418.22 for (1) of (1) clinical record reviewed during an interdisciplinary team meeting (IDT) (CR14). The registered nurse composed the initial certification while reviewing and reading the clinical record to the medical director (MD) during a teleconferenced IDT.

Findings included:

Surveyor attended IDT on December 15, 2021, at 10 a.m. The team (administrator, registered nurses, social worker, and chaplain) met in-person at agency office while the medical director attended remotely from a Hospital in Farrell (owned by same company) appearing on an opened laptop computer. At 10:28 a.m., EMP3 (registered nurse) began reading information to the medical director from CR14 and the MD could be heard typing on his/her computer keyboard and said, "ok tell me a story." At this time, surveyor began taking notes as to what EMP3 told the MD during the meeting. EMP3 continued to read and noted one of CR14's diagnoses to the MD was "poly neuropathy" to which the medical director replied, "other musculoskeletal findings ... want me to put that?" EMP3 then noted "unrelated UTI [urinary tract infection]" to which the MD replied and typed, "I'll put history of [UTI]." EMP3 kept reading while the MD typed and the MD would interject with, "Got it," and "OK." The medical director then concluded as he/she continued to type, "I expect his [CR14] prognosis to be 6 months or less."

After IDT was completed, surveyor interviewed the medical director with EMP1 (administrator) at 11:25 a.m. The MD confirmed the nurses compose the initial certification of terminal illness by reading the clinical record information to him/her. When asked why he/she relied on the nurses to review the record for him/her he/she noted that it's because the agency's electronic medical record is difficult to use and "it takes too long," and "it's a waste of my time ... they [nurses] can read and speak faster." 

At 11:39 a.m., surveyor interviewed another nurse (EMP2) who was present during team since EMP3 had left. He/she confirmed that the registered nurses read and review the clinical record for the MD while he/she types the narrative for initial certification of terminal illness. 

Review of CR14 on December 17, 2021, at 11 a.m. showed an admission date of 12/9/2021 for an initial certification period ending 3/8/2022. Review of CR14's "HOSPICE CERTIFICATION OF TERMINAL ILLNESS" showed the "Narrative composed by Hospice Physician" contained the same information read to him/her by EMP3 during the 12/15/2021 IDT meeting. The narrative was electronically authenticated by the MD on 12/16/2021 at 7:15 a.m. to show that, according to the certification document, "By signing this certification, the hospice Physician, named below, confirms that he/she composed the narrative based on his/her review of the patient's medical record or his/her examination of the patient." 

Interview with EMP1 during the above clinical record review confirmed findings. At this time, EMP1 also confirmed that the MD had not examined the patient either when he/she noted that a face-to-face encounter had not yet been done.
